activities.title: Core Mechanics: Access Modifiers & The Complete Access Matrix
activities.content:
Encapsulation is one of the foundational pillars of Object-Oriented Programming. If every field and method in an application were accessible to everyone, maintaining system integrity would be impossible. Java provides **Access Modifiers** to enforce clear visibility boundaries between classes, packages, and external consumers.

### 1. The 4 Access Levels in Java
Java provides 4 distinct visibility tiers:
1. **`public`**: Accessible from anywhere in the world (any class in any package).
2. **`protected`**: Accessible within the same package, AND by subclasses in different packages through inheritance.
3. **Default (Package-Private)**: Accessible ONLY within the same package. There is no `default` modifier keyword; you specify it by omitting any modifier!
4. **`private`**: Accessible ONLY within the exact same enclosing class.

### 2. The Definitive Java Access Matrix
This table is one of the most frequently tested concepts in Java technical interviews:

| Location / Context | `public` | `protected` | Default (Package-Private) | `private` |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Same Class | YES | YES | YES | YES |
| Same Package (Non-subclass) | YES | YES | YES | NO |
| Same Package (Subclass) | YES | YES | YES | NO |
| Different Package (Subclass) | YES | YES | NO | NO |
| Different Package (World / Non-subclass) | YES | NO | NO | NO |

### 3. Permitted Modifiers for Top-Level Classes
A top-level class (a class declared directly in a `.java` file, not nested inside another class) can **ONLY** have two access levels:
1. **`public`**: Accessible to classes in all packages. Must match the `.java` filename.
2. **Default (Package-Private)**: No modifier keyword. Accessible only to classes in the same package.

*A top-level class CANNOT be `private` or `protected`*! Doing so triggers a compile-time error: `modifier private not allowed here`.

### 4. Why Package-Private Matters
Many beginners assume everything should be `public` or `private`. However, **package-private** is the secret weapon for modular design:
- It allows classes inside the same package to collaborate closely and access each other's internal helper methods.
- It hides those internal implementation details completely from outside packages, keeping your public API surface clean and indestructible.

activities.title: Concept Check & MCQ: Access Modifiers & The Complete Access Matrix

questions.question: What is the access level of a class member declared without any access modifier (e.g. `int count;`)?
options: private
protected
default (package-private)
public
questions.explanation: Omitting an access modifier in Java assigns default package-private visibility, accessible only within the same package.

questions.question: Which access modifiers are permitted for a top-level (non-nested) Java class?
options: public, protected, default, and private
public and default (package-private) only
public and private only
public only
questions.explanation: Top-level classes can only be public or package-private. They cannot be marked private or protected.

questions.question: Can a subclass in a DIFFERENT package access a `protected` member of its superclass?
options: No, protected is strictly within the same package
Yes, protected members are inherited and accessible to subclasses across packages
Only if the member is static
Only using reflection
questions.explanation: protected explicitly grants access to subclasses in other packages through inheritance.

questions.question: Can a non-subclass in a different package access a `protected` member?
options: Yes, protected is the same as public
No, protected members are completely inaccessible to unrelated classes outside the package
Yes, if it imports the package
Only if the JVM is in developer mode
questions.explanation: Unrelated classes outside the package cannot access protected members.

questions.question: When overriding a method, what rule governs the access modifier of the overriding method?
options: The overriding method can have any access modifier
The overriding method cannot reduce the visibility of the superclass method (it can only maintain or broaden it)
The overriding method must always be marked private
The overriding method must have narrower visibility
questions.explanation: An overriding method cannot reduce visibility (e.g. overriding a public method as protected or private is illegal in Java).

questions.question: Why is there no explicit `default` keyword for package-private member declarations?
options: Because default is reserved for switch statements (and later interface default methods)
Because Java developers forgot to add it
Because package-private is deprecated
Because it is only allowed in interfaces
questions.explanation: In Java syntax, package-private is represented by the absence of a modifier because `default` was a reserved keyword for switch statements.

questions.question: Which of the following members is accessible from ANY class in ANY package?
options: protected int id;
public int id;
int id;
private int id;
questions.explanation: public members are accessible from all classes across all packages without restriction.

questions.question: What is the primary architectural purpose of package-private visibility?
options: To optimize JVM bytecode execution
To allow related classes within a cohesive package to collaborate while hiding internal implementation details from external packages
To prevent classes from being garbage collected
To satisfy compiler warnings
questions.explanation: Package-private creates package-level encapsulation, allowing classes to share internal logic without exposing it to outside packages.

activities.title: Interview Q&A: Access Modifiers & The Complete Access Matrix

interviewQA.question: Recite the complete Java Access Matrix across all 4 modifiers and 5 access contexts.
interviewQA.answer:
| Context | public | protected | default | private |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Same Class | YES | YES | YES | YES |
| Same Package (Non-subclass) | YES | YES | YES | NO |
| Same Package (Subclass) | YES | YES | YES | NO |
| Different Package (Subclass) | YES | YES | NO | NO |
| Different Package (World) | YES | NO | NO | NO |

interviewQA.question: Why does Java forbid top-level classes from being declared `private` or `protected`?
interviewQA.answer: A top-level class exists directly at the package level. Marking a top-level class `private` would mean no other class in the universe could ever instantiate or reference it, making it completely useless. Marking it `protected` would make no sense because packages do not have inheritance relationships. Therefore, only `public` (accessible everywhere) or default (accessible within the package) make logical sense for top-level classes.

interviewQA.question: Explain the rule governing access modifier visibility during method overriding.
interviewQA.answer:
An overriding method cannot reduce the visibility of the superclass method (Liskov Substitution Principle). For example:
- A `public` method can ONLY be overridden as `public`.
- A `protected` method can be overridden as `protected` or `public`.
- A package-private method can be overridden as package-private, `protected`, or `public`.
Attempting to narrow visibility (e.g. overriding `public void run()` with `protected void run()`) causes a compile error: `attempting to assign weaker access privileges`.

interviewQA.question: How does `protected` access work across packages when referencing an instance of the superclass?
interviewQA.answer: This is a famous Java edge case! In a subclass in a different package, you can access protected members through inheritance (`this.protectedField` or `super.protectedField`). However, you **CANNOT** access a protected member on a reference to the superclass object itself (`SuperClass obj = new SuperClass(); obj.protectedField;` -> COMPILE ERROR!). The subclass only has access through its own inherited lineage.

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between package-private visibility and protected visibility?
interviewQA.answer: `package-private` (default) restricts access strictly to classes within the exact same package. `protected` provides package-private access PLUS cross-package access for subclasses that inherit from the class. In short: `protected` = package-private + inheritance across packages.

interviewQA.question: Can a private method in a superclass be overridden in a subclass?
interviewQA.answer: No! Private methods are completely invisible outside their declaring class and are not inherited by subclasses. If a subclass declares a method with the identical signature, it is an entirely new, unrelated method that **hides** (not overrides) the private method. Adding `@Override` on that subclass method will cause a compilation error.

interviewQA.question: Why should instance variables almost always be declared `private`?
interviewQA.answer: Declaring fields `private` enforces **encapsulation**. It prevents external classes from directly manipulating internal state without validation, prevents tight coupling between components, and allows the internal data structure to be refactored without breaking external client code.
